subject: Business
title: The ABC Analysis of Inventory
description: A 60-second lesson on The ABC Analysis of Inventory.

hook.text: A warehouse has 10,000 SKUs. Managing each one equally is impossible. Some matter far more than others.

buildup.text: ABC analysis classifies inventory: A items (20% of SKUs, 80% of value), B items (30%, 15%), C items (50%, 5%).

discovery.text: A items get tight control, frequent reviews, and accurate forecasting. C items get simple replenishment rules.

twist.text: Treating all items equally wastes resources on low-value items while under-managing critical ones.

climax.text: A hospital applied ABC analysis: critical medications (A) got daily checks; office supplies (C) got monthly orders.

punchline.text: Not all inventory is equal. Manage accordingly.

quiz.question: In ABC analysis, what characterizes 'A' items?
options: They represent about 20% of SKUs but 80% of total value
They are the cheapest items in the warehouse

details.summary: ABC analysis classifies inventory into three categories based on value and volume: A items are high-value products needing tight control, B items are moderate, and C items are low-value goods managed with simpler systems. It applies the Pareto principle to inventory.
details.whyItMatters: Not all inventory deserves equal attention. ABC analysis focuses management effort and capital on the 20 percent of items that typically represent 80 percent of value, preventing costly stockouts of critical products while simplifying oversight of
takeaways: A items represent roughly 20% of SKUs but 80% of inventory value
B items are moderate in both value and volume, needing balanced control
C items are numerous but low-value, managed with simple reorder rules

faq.question: How do you classify items into A, B, and C categories?
faq.answer: Multiply each item's unit cost by annual demand to get total annual value. Rank all items by this value. Typically the top 10-20% by value are A items, the next 20-30% are B items, and the remaining 50-70% are C items. Exact thresholds vary by industry.

faq.question: What management strategies differ between A, B, and C items?
faq.answer: A items get frequent cycle counts, tight safety stock calculations, and close supplier relationships. B items use periodic review and moderate safety stock. C items use simple min-max reorder systems with larger safety stock since the cost of control exceeds item value.
